name: custom-hook
intent: Extract reusable stateful behaviour — state plus the effects that keep it synchronized — into a plain function that a component invokes, so unrelated components share the logic without a mixin, a wrapper component or a base class.
problem: Several unrelated components need the same stateful logic (subscribe to a browser or platform API, fetch with loading and error states, validate a form, debounce a value), but the state and its effect wiring are entangled with one component's markup. Copying the logic duplicates the cleanup path, and the classic reuse mechanisms force the consumer into a wrapper (higher-order component), a render-prop callback or an inheritance/mixin structure — all of which distort the component tree and hide the logic just as much as the duplication did.
context: Component-based UI codebases whose runtime owns state slots and drives re-rendering from state changes (React and Vue Composition API on the web, Jetpack Compose on Android, SwiftUI on Apple platforms), where behaviour must be shared between components that have no other relationship. It applies whenever state plus lifecycle effects form a unit of reuse that is independent of any particular visual output; it does not apply to stateless helpers, which should remain ordinary functions.
benefits: Stateful logic is written once and called by any number of unrelated components; consumers add no wrapper element and no base class to their tree.
The consumer's component body reads as intent — use the online status — instead of mechanism (add these listeners, remember to remove them).
Cleanup travels with the logic: the effect teardown is written once, so subscription, timer and observer leaks are fixed for every call site at the same time.
Units compose directly with units: a hook can call other hooks, letting a specialized behaviour be assembled from smaller pieces without diamond resolution or inheritance-order rules.
Each call site owns an independent state instance, so a shared helper cannot accidentally couple two components' state.
The extracted unit is testable in isolation with a small harness, independently of the components that render it.
No wrapper nesting in DevTools, unlike HOCs; the component tree stays flat and debuggable.
Better TypeScript inference than HOCs — return shapes are plain function return types, not inferred-through-wrapper generics.
Works across completely different component types (a form and a table can both call useFetch) without prop drilling.
tradeoffs: The call-order discipline (only at the top level of a component or another hook) is a convention enforced by lint and review, not by the type system; violating it displaces state slots and produces confusing cross-wired bugs.
The unit is only valid inside the host runtime's render, so it cannot be called from plain functions, and unit tests need a renderer harness or a dedicated hook-testing library.
Returned values and callbacks must be identity-stable (memoised or keyed); getting that wrong silently re-runs effects or leaves listeners holding stale state.
Inputs can become invisible: a unit that reads context, global stores or module state removes dependencies from the component's props, so debugging means reading the whole hook chain.
It is not a state-sharing mechanism — two call sites get two independent states; teams that expect shared state must switch to a context or store pattern.
The unit body executes on every render, and stable identities plus memoisation add bookkeeping and allocation that a direct inline implementation would not need.
A custom hook cannot provide a stable identity for a single logical piece of external shared state — that requires useSyncExternalStore, Context, or an external store.

participants.responsibility: Invokes the unit at the top level of its render, owns the instance's lifetime and renders the returned state and actions; it never sees the internal mechanics.

Plain function named for its intent that composes the runtime's state and effect primitives and returns the value/action surface; pure with respect to its inputs, with side effects confined to effect registrations.

Framework-provided state slots and effect scheduler: stores per-call-site state keyed by invocation order, re-runs the host when state changes, and runs or cancels effect callbacks with the host's lifecycle.
Other hooks, composables or built-in primitives (state, context, derived values, external-store subscription) that the unit calls; composition happens by direct calls, with no wrapper.
The returned tuple or object — state values plus stable callbacks — that the host renders and that sibling units build on; it hides the mechanism and is the unit's public interface.

use_cases: Exposing a browser or platform capability as reactive state: online status, window size, media-query match, geolocation, app foreground state, dark mode, reduced-motion preference.
Data fetching with loading, error and refresh semantics (a useQuery-style unit) reused by list, detail and search components; including cancellation via AbortController.
Form state and validation shared by unrelated forms, including touched/dirty tracking, field-level errors, submit handling and reset.
Debounced or throttled derived values (search boxes, resize handlers) with correct timer cleanup and leading/trailing edge options.

Subscribing to an external reactive store (Redux-style store, WebSocket, EventSource, SSE, platform service) and mapping snapshots into component state; using useSyncExternalStore for tear-free reads.
Timers, polling and animations whose start and stop must be tied to the component lifetime; including pause/resume semantics.
Cross-cutting checks such as permissions, feature flags or entitlement checks that combine context values with local state.
Animation and transition state derived from scroll position, pointer proximity or layout metrics.
Encapsulating a specific third-party library or browser API behind a declarative interface (e.g., Web Audio API, Battery Status, Vibration API).
Abstracting away SSR guards and window/document checks so consumers receive a client-only reactive value without needing to know the platform detail.
Capturing and persisting UI state across sessions: localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB-backed state with hydration.

Library APIs delivered as hook calls instead of injected props or wrapper components: TanStack Query exposes fetching, caching and synchronising server state as useQuery; React Router exposes routing as useParams, useNavigate and useLocation.
Curated composable ecosystems shipped as versioned packages: VueUse's 200+ Vue composables (useMouse, useLocalStorage, createSharedComposable) built tree-shakeable, TypeScript-first and SSR-friendly.
avoid_when: The logic has no state or effects: write a plain function and keep the hook naming convention off it — React's guidance is explicit that functions which do not call hooks should not be hooks.
Only one component needs the behaviour today: inline it until a second real consumer appears; premature extraction adds an indirection someone must maintain.
The components must observe one shared state instance: that is shared state, so use a store or context/provider pattern instead of a unit that only looks like it shares.
The reuse is structural or visual (layout, styling, markup shape): component composition, compound components or a wrapper/modifier is the right mechanism.
There is no host runtime that re-renders on state change (batch jobs, request handlers, plain library code): a state-holder object or a plain closure API fits better.
The behaviour is a pure derivation of props with no side effects: use useMemo or a plain const — a hook adds overhead and conceals the fact that no state exists.
You are wrapping a single primitive with no added semantics (a useToggle around one useState) — naming ceremony without abstraction; the indirection cost exceeds the savings.
anti_patterns: conditional-hook-call: Calling hooks conditionally, in loops, or from event handlers and plain functions: state slots shift between renders and previously independent states cross-wire. Fix: restructure so all hooks in a component call unconditionally; gate logic inside the hook body with conditionals, not around the call.

kitchen-sink-hook: One hook that owns fetching, routing, formatting and unrelated UI state — every consumer pays for all of it. Fix: split into focused hooks (useFetch, useRouter, useFormatter) and compose them in a single usePageData that the page component calls.

primitive-wrapper: Wrapping a single built-in with no added semantics (a useToggle around one useState) — naming ceremony without abstraction; the indirection cost exceeds the savings. Exception: only extract when a second real consumer actually exists or the abstraction carries a clear semantic name.

stateless-helper-as-hook: Mislabelling a stateless helper as a hook so it can no longer be called conditionally, or under-labelling a real hook so callers treat it as a plain function. Functions that don't call any hooks should never start with use; the prefix is what makes the linter enforce the Rules of Hooks on the body.

assumed-shared-state: Assuming two components calling the same unit share state, then debugging why their updates do not propagate. Custom hooks share logic, not state — each call site is fully independent. When shared state is genuinely needed, the hook must read from a context or external store.

silenced-dependency-lint: Silencing the exhaustive-deps lint instead of fixing effect dependencies leaves effects that either never re-run when inputs change or loop infinitely. Treat every lint warning as a bug until proven otherwise; refactor the effect body or the dependency array.

hidden-global-access: Hiding surprising global, context or storage access inside the unit so the host cannot reason about the unit's dependencies. Fix: surface all inputs as explicit parameters or document them; a well-designed hook is a readable contract, not a hidden implementation.

lifecycle-wrappers: Creating convenience hooks like useMount, useEffectOnce or useUpdateEffect that wrap useEffect with an empty or partial dependency array. These hide dependencies from the linter, suppress meaningful warnings, and misrepresent React's model — it synchronises, it does not have lifecycle events. Write the Effect directly; the linter will catch missing dependencies.

unstable-return-values: Returning a new object or array on every render without memoisation (e.g., return { value, toggle } where both are fresh references each render). Consumers that destructure or list the return in a dependency array will churn unnecessarily. Wrap with useMemo / useCallback as appropriate, or enable the React Compiler.

missing-ssr-guard: Accessing window, document, localStorage, matchMedia or other browser-only APIs during the hook's body (not inside an effect) causes 'window is not defined' crashes in SSR/SSG frameworks. Guard with typeof window !== 'undefined' in the initializer, or move browser reads into an effect with a safe default for the server.

forgotten-cleanup: Not returning a cleanup function from useEffect that removes listeners, cancels timers, disconnects observers or aborts in-flight requests. Causes memory leaks and state updates on unmounted components. Return a cleanup from every effect that registers side effects; use AbortController for fetch, matching removeEventListener for listeners, and clearTimeout for timers.

god-hook-parameters: A hook that accepts 10+ parameters or returns 10+ values, exposing every internal state setter and scratch value. This exposes rather than encapsulates — the caller can tamper with internal state that should be managed. Return only readable state values and semantic action functions; hide internal setters and intermediate values.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: stateful behaviour is separated from rendering — the host draws, the unit manages state and effects.
Composition over inheritance: units compose by direct calls instead of extending classes, wrapping components or layering mixins.
Single source of truth for repeated logic: one implementation of a behaviour, reused rather than copied.
Information hiding: the returned surface exposes intent-level values and actions while the mechanism (subscriptions, timers, storage) stays private.
Explicit lifetime ownership: the host owns the instance, the runtime owns the slots, and cleanup is declared together with the effect.
Purity at the boundary: the unit's body is a pure function of its inputs, with mutations confined to the runtime's state setters and effects.

Hook by problem boundary, not by technical layer: split on what the logic solves (a search capability, a chat room) rather than on useState vs useEffect lines; the hook should answer 'what complete problem does this solve?'
Explicit over implicit inputs: surface context reads, global store reads and storage access as parameters or document them so the host can reason about dependencies.
Return surface minimisation: return only what the consumer needs — readable state plus semantic actions; hide internal setters and intermediate scratch values.
best_practices: Name the unit for its intent using the ecosystem's convention (use prefix in React and Vue, rememberX in Compose) and keep one responsibility per unit. If naming is hard, the unit may not have a clear boundary yet.

Design the call site before the body: write the desired usage (parameters, return shape) first; the implementation then fills in to satisfy that contract. This prevents 'add one more thing' drift and keeps the surface tight.
Return a tuple for 1–2 related values (mirrors useState); return an object for 3+ or when meaning is named. Use const assertions on tuples to preserve label inference at call sites.

Keep the body pure during render; perform subscriptions and interactions in effects with teardown. Never create listeners, timers or subscriptions at module scope or during render — only inside effects.

Stabilise identities for values and callbacks that feed effects or memoised children: wrap returned functions in useCallback, memoised objects in useMemo. With React Compiler enabled this is automatic; without it, this is still required.
Use the runtime's built-in primitives (state, context, useSyncExternalStore, derived via useMemo) over re-implementing them inside the unit.
Cancel in-flight async work with AbortController on dependency-change and on unmount; late responses must not overwrite stale state.
Handle SSR explicitly: guard browser-API reads (window, document, localStorage, matchMedia) with typeof window !== 'undefined' or move them into effects with a safe server-side default.

Prefer the options-object parameter pattern past 1–2 arguments so call sites remain readable and options can be added without breaking existing callers: useFetch(url, { enabled, refetchInterval, debounce }) not useFetch(url, true, 5000, false).
Keep pure computation out of the hook body — extract it into a plain function the hook wraps, so it can be unit tested without a renderer harness.
Surface hidden inputs (context, stores, storage keys) as explicit parameters or document them in the hook's JSDoc/TSDoc so consumers and reviewers understand what the hook reads from outside itself.

Test the contract, not the implementation: given inputs and options, assert returned state and side effects. Use the framework's renderHook utility; control time with fake timers for debounce/throttle tests. Mock network boundaries; don't rely on real APIs.
Use discriminated unions or specific status fields (data/error/isLoading) rather than null for async state so TypeScript can narrow types correctly through the status.
Prefer useSyncExternalStore over a manual useState+useEffect subscription pattern for external stores — it is tear-free and handles concurrent rendering correctly.
Wrap event handlers received as props inside useEffectEvent (React 19+) to read the latest value without making the effect reactive to every parent re-render.

Design hooks at the problem-boundary level: useSearchQuery (not useState+useEffect+useDebounce separately); let the hook encode the team's conventions so callers simply use the value without needing to know how debouncing is configured.

When extracting: only do so when the same useState+useEffect pattern appears in two or more real components — not preemptively for a one-off. The right time to extract is when the boundary has emerged, not when code has just gotten long.
Keep hooks focused on one concrete high-level use case. If the name requires 'and' (useFetchAndTransformAndCache), split it. Small focused hooks compose; large ones couple.

related_patterns_notes.higher-order-component: predecessor — HOCs were the primary mechanism for sharing stateful behaviour before hooks; custom hooks solve the same problem without wrapper nesting, prop collisions or DevTools pollution; when_to_use_together: When wrapping a class component or third-party component tree where hooks cannot be inserted; or when a cross-cutting behaviour must be injected without the consumer calling a hook
related_patterns_notes.render-props: predecessor — render props shared stateful logic via a child function; hooks replace this with a direct function call that avoids the child-prop pyramid and type-inference complexity; when_to_use_together: When a library API genuinely needs to control part of the child rendering tree (e.g., virtualisers, animation libs); or when a hook cannot be inserted into the consumer's component
related_patterns_notes.compound-components: complementary — compound components own visual composition and implicit state sharing; a custom hook inside each compound child can own the behaviour side while the pattern owns the markup structure; when_to_use_together: When a composable API shape (like a Tabs or Select) also needs internal stateful behaviour shared between the parent and children without prop drilling
related_patterns_notes.headless-component: complementary — a headless component provides behaviour-only (no markup) via slots or render props; a custom hook extracts the same behaviour to be callable directly without the wrapper component; when_to_use_together: When the behaviour needs to be shared both as a callable hook and as a drop-in wrapper component for consumers that prefer the component API
related_patterns_notes.context-provider: enabler — context provides the shared-state broadcasting that a custom hook reads when it surfaces app-wide state (theme, auth, locale); the hook is the consumer interface, the provider is the mechanism; when_to_use_together: When the behaviour needs to observe shared state that changes rarely but broadly (auth session, theme, feature flags)
related_patterns_notes.presentational-vs-container: architectural alignment — the container/presentational split (data-fetching vs rendering) maps directly onto custom hooks: containers become hooks, presentational components become pure consumers; when_to_use_together: When migrating a legacy container/presentational codebase — extract container logic into hooks and keep the presentational component as a pure renderer
related_patterns_notes.props-drilling: alternative to avoid — props drilling passes state down through intermediate components that never use it; a custom hook short-circuits the chain by letting any leaf component call the hook directly; when_to_use_together: When a leaf component needs state that multiple intermediate layers don't use, and refactoring the component tree is impractical
related_patterns_notes.state-colocation: principle — hooks encourage state to live at the narrowest appropriate scope; the pattern's independence guarantee (each call site owns its own state) reinforces colocation by default; when_to_use_together: Always — keep hook state scoped to the component that renders it unless explicit shared state (context/store) is required
